note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §13.7, Stage 90; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiments 12 and C14) on data/benches/flames.json: the burner's flame with its air shut and open; flame tests of seven salts read by eye and by the spectral viewer (atomic lines: sodium, lithium, potassium; monohydroxide bands: calcium, strontium, barium, copper); potassium's faint lilac in a dimmed room; sodium hiding potassium; two unknowns; a photon's energy.
title: Experiment: flame tests and their spectra

report.label: sodium's yellow line
report.why: NIST: the D lines at 588.995 and 589.592 nm in air; the viewer reads to the nanometre.

report.label: lithium's red line
report.why: NIST: 670.776 and 670.791 nm, the 2p to 2s line's two components.

report.label: potassium's brighter red line
report.why: NIST: 766.490 nm (and 769.896 nm, its partner): 4p to 4s.

report.label: the energy of a mole of photons of sodium's line
report.why: E = N_A h c / lambda = (6.022e23 /mol)(6.626e-34 J s)(2.998e8 m/s) / 589.3e-9 m = 203.0 kJ/mol, 2.10 eV a photon: the energy between sodium's 3p and 3s levels.

report.label: the crimson flame with bands at 606 and 682 nm
report.why: Strontium's SrOH bands; lithium's crimson is a single line at 671 nm.

report.label: the green flame brightest at 546 nm
report.why: Copper's CuOH bands run from 505 to 546 nm; barium's BaOH are brightest at 513 and 524.

report.label: what the mixture holds
report.why: Sodium and potassium: yellow to the eye, and potassium's 766 and 770 nm lines in the viewer.

report.label: unknown X
report.why: Its colour and its lines against the seven you noted.

report.label: unknown Y
report.why: Its colour and its lines against the seven you noted.

steps.title: A small flame
steps.text: Right-click the burner and open its valve only a little, under a third. A small, lazy flame: yellow, because its gas burns short of air and the soot in it glows.
steps.why: The yellow of a candle or a burner with its air shut is glowing soot: carbon specks at the flame's temperature, a smooth spectrum like a lamp filament's, no lines.

steps.title: Wide open
steps.text: Drag the valve wide open. The flame turns blue: with air mixed in, the gas burns clean, and the blue comes from molecular fragments of the burning gas, not from any metal.
steps.why: A flame test needs this hot, nearly colourless flame (about 1900 C here), so that what colours it is only what the loop brings.

steps.title: The probe in the flame
steps.text: Drag the spectral viewer's probe from its holder into the flame. Right-click the viewer: its screen shows the flame's light at every nanometre, and it lists any lines it finds.
steps.why: The burner's own light is weak and spread out. Each metal you put in it adds light at its own wavelengths, sharp lines from atoms and wider bands from molecules.

steps.title: Sodium
steps.text: Pick up the sodium chloride and click the burner: a loop dipped in it is held in the flame. A blazing yellow. Look at the viewer's screen: nearly all of that light is in one place.
steps.why: Sodium's atoms, excited in the flame, fall back from their first excited level and give out the D lines, 589.0 and 589.6 nm. They are so bright that a trace of sodium (from fingers, from dust, from glass) colours any flame yellow.

steps.title: Na's line in the notebook
steps.text: Right-click the viewer and read its lines. In the notebook, write the label Na and the wavelength of sodium's yellow line, in nanometres.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again: the sodium burns away in a few seconds. Each test starts from a clean flame, so that what you see is only what the loop brings (speed the clock up if you like).

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: Lithium
steps.text: Pick up the lithium chloride and click the burner. A crimson flame. Read the viewer: one strong line, deep in the red.
steps.why: Lithium's resonance line is at 670.8 nm. A weaker line at 610 nm sits beside it, and the eye sees the sum as crimson.

steps.title: Li's line in the notebook
steps.text: In the notebook, write the label Li and the wavelength of lithium's red line.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: The lights down
steps.text: Potassium's colour is famously faint. Click "lights" in the top bar until the room is at 10 % or less: your eye opens up to the dimmer room as a pupil would, and whatever makes its own light stands out against it.

checks.text: the room's lights at 10 % or less

steps.why: Against a dimmer room, everything that makes its own light looks brighter: that is why flame tests are watched in a darkened lab.

steps.title: Potassium
steps.text: Pick up the potassium chloride and click the burner. Look closely: even in the dark the flame stays nearly its own blue, a hint of lilac at most. The viewer shows why: its brightest lines are deep red, at the very edge of what the eye can see.
steps.why: Potassium's resonance lines are at 766.5 and 769.9 nm, where the eye is nearly blind; a weak violet pair at 404.4 and 404.7 nm is all it adds to the blue. A chemist looks through cobalt-blue glass, which stops the burner's and sodium's light and passes potassium's deep red: the viewer does the same job by wavelength.

steps.title: K's line in the notebook
steps.text: In the notebook, write the label K and the wavelength of potassium's brighter red line.

steps.title: The lights up
steps.text: Click "lights" in the top bar until the room is at its full light again.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: Calcium
steps.text: Pick up the calcium chloride and click the burner. Brick red. The viewer shows wider humps instead of sharp lines.
steps.why: Calcium in a flame is mostly calcium monohydroxide, CaOH: a molecule's light comes in bands a few nanometres wide, here mostly orange-red at 622 nm with a green band at 555 nm. Calcium's own atomic line at 423 nm is weak. (A faint line at 766 nm may linger: the last trace of potassium, which the viewer still sees and the eye does not.)

steps.title: Ca's band in the notebook
steps.text: Right-click the viewer: it names the peak of what it sees. In the notebook, write the label Ca and the peak's wavelength.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: Strontium
steps.text: Pick up the strontium chloride and click the burner. A crimson as deep as lithium's, but the viewer sees something else: several bands, from orange to deep red.
steps.why: Strontium monohydroxide, SrOH, gives bands at 606, 659, 671 and 682 nm. To the eye strontium and lithium are both crimson; the spectrum tells them apart at once.

steps.title: Sr's band in the notebook
steps.text: In the notebook, write the label Sr and the wavelength of the viewer's peak. Compare it with lithium's line.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: Barium
steps.text: Pick up the barium chloride and click the burner. A pale apple green.
steps.why: Barium monohydroxide's bands, 513 and 524 nm in the green and 488 nm in the blue-green, with barium's own atomic line at 553.5 nm standing sharp among them. Barium salts give green fireworks.

steps.title: Ba's band in the notebook
steps.text: In the notebook, write the label Ba and the wavelength of the viewer's peak: barium's own atomic line, sharper than the bands around it.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: Copper
steps.text: Pick up the copper(II) sulfate and click the burner. A green again, but a different green: the viewer puts it at other wavelengths.
steps.why: Copper's green comes from copper monohydroxide, CuOH: bands from 505 to 546 nm, brightest at 546. Copper's own atoms are barely excited at this temperature.

steps.title: Cu's band in the notebook
steps.text: In the notebook, write the label Cu and the wavelength of the viewer's peak: a green of its own, not barium's.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: A mixture
steps.text: Pick up the mixture of sodium and potassium chlorides and click the burner. Yellow: just sodium, to the eye. Now read the viewer's lines.
steps.why: Sodium's yellow swamps potassium's faint lilac. A chemist looks through cobalt-blue glass, which absorbs the yellow; the spectral viewer does better and still lists potassium's lines at 766 and 770 nm beside sodium's 589.

steps.title: The mixture's lines in the notebook
steps.text: Right-click the viewer and read its lines. In the notebook, write the label mix and the longest wavelength it lists: a line the eye cannot see in that yellow.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again. A clean flame, before each unknown, so that what you see is only what it brings.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: Unknown X
steps.text: Pick up unknown X and click the burner. Its colour, and the viewer's lines, say which of the seven it is: compare them with what you noted.
steps.why: Yellow and 589 nm: sodium. Crimson with one line at 671: lithium. Crimson with bands at 606 and 682: strontium. Brick red with a band at 622: calcium. Lilac with 766 and 770: potassium. Green at 513 and 524: barium. Green brightest at 546: copper.

steps.title: The flame clears
steps.text: Wait until the flame is its own blue again.

checks.text: the flame its own blue again

steps.title: Unknown Y
steps.text: Pick up unknown Y and click the burner, and name it the same way.
steps.why: Two unknowns may be the same salt: each was drawn on its own.
